body.text: In brief
• An Australian Palestinian man helped bring Nippers to Gaza in 2023, but the program was halted by war.
• Now, it's resumed for the first time, in an event he says brought a rare opportunity for hope, joy and fun and learning.
A group of kids gathered on a beach last month to take part in Nippers, a beloved childhood tradition for generations of Australians.

But in the three years since the children last met, war has turned their lives upside down. Some members of the original group are believed to have died. Others have lost their homes or family members, or can no longer be contacted.
Australian Palestinian man Shamikh Badra, who brought Gaza its first Nippers program, told SBS News its return was a "message of hope" for children who had endured so much.
"For a few moments, the scene looked simple: children running on the sand, playing, learning and enjoying themselves near the sea," Badra said.
"The feedback was amazing. They were happy, and they said we are so happy that we finally started the Nippers again, and the new children are happy too."
Around 50 kids participated. Before the war, roughly 45 children were part of the program, Badra said, but the team could only reach 15 of the original group.
How did Nippers land in Gaza?
Badra once worked as a lifeguard in Gaza, and loved its "beautiful" 45km shoreline.
After moving to Sydney in 2014, he found joy in seeing children enjoy Australia's shores and learn lifesaving and beach education through the Nippers program.

In 2017, he embarked on a years-long journey to give kids in Gaza a similar experience, navigating a maze of visa and logistical complexities to eventually bring two Palestinians to train at Sydney's North Steyne Surf Lifesavers Club in December 2019.
After obtaining surf lifesaving qualifications through the club, the men returned home to establish the Gaza Beach Surf Lifesaving Club.
But its start was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Finally, in mid-2023, Gaza Nippers began its first season. But it was only active for a short time before war put it on hold.
On 7 October 2023, the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel left 1,200 people dead and 251 taken captive.
Israel's subsequent bombardment of Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people and wounded 175,000, according to the local health ministry.

At least 21,7000 children have been killed since the war began, according to UNICEF, including at least 300 since a ceasefire was announced in October last year. An estimated 1.7 million children are in need of humanitarian assistance.
A return against all odds
On 25 September, the team behind Gaza Nippers hosted its first session since the war began.
"Before the war, Gaza Nippers was mainly a project about water safety, sport and teamwork. But what the children have lived through since then has given its return another meaning," Badra said.
"We are not presenting one day on the beach as a treatment for what these children have experienced.

"A sports program cannot bring back a destroyed home, a family member who was lost, or years of interrupted education. But it can bring back some simple and important things in a child’s life: a place to go, an activity to look forward to, other children to meet, something new to learn."
With much of Gaza in ruins, it was not easy to bring the program back together.
Christine Stewart works at the North Steyne Surf Life Saving Club and sits on the Northern Beaches Committee for Palestine, which raises money for the Gaza Nippers program.
She said the local organisers of the program had great difficulty piecing together the resources and overcoming safety fears and other barriers to resuming the program.
"We tried to find some of the materials from 2023. Most of them have been destroyed or stolen or are no longer available.
"So they had to really do a lot of stuff from scratch and put that all together in an environment where you can't find things, where it's very expensive to find materials."
"The fact that they were able to hold it in the first place is a miracle."
'An Australian way of life'
Stewart said Nippers is "kind of like a rite of passage" for Australian kids to learn about surf safety.

"It's very uniquely Australian, and to then take this tradition, take this very ingrained cultural part of Australia and translate that to Gaza and enable kids then to enjoy the beach, to learn these skills, ... is just a really wonderful thing."
It provided the children with an opportunity to "just be kids" for a few hours, she added.
With Gaza headed into its winter months, the program will likely pause for now, with hopes to start it back up on a regular basis next year.
"We should not give up," Badra said.
"We should not allow these children to be afraid all the time."
"This is a symbolic message that we will continue to help and support."
